metadata.title: Glasgow Y-DNA Explorer
metadata.scope: Reanalysis of supplied Y-DNA page and additional project timeline; historical synthesis and matrix audit, without fresh raw-read, live-clade or pedigree verification.

roots.name: Henry Glasgo
roots.note: Two separate tests are associated with this reported root. Only the unnumbered Big Y is assigned to FT25406; 325862 remains SNP-unresolved.

roots.name: James William Glasgow
roots.note: Candidate mapping to the Kilwaughter/Larne James William. Its Y-37 pairing with 325862 is a testable lead, not an SNP placement.

roots.name: Robert Glasgow
roots.note: Candidate mapping to Robert c.1710, spouse Rachel Wilson. An especially useful East Antrim line for testing against the SNP tree.

roots.name: John Glasgow
roots.note: Candidate mapping to John, spouse Mary Arthur. The Y-67 panel does not include DYS712 or DYS714.

roots.name: Reported William line
roots.note: B696189 is assigned to FT20271. The claimed descent from William c.1655 has not been independently validated here. The source mentions an additional unnumbered Y-111 test whose identity is not reconciled.

roots.name: James J Glasgow line
roots.route: South Carolina → Giles County, Tennessee → Pontotoc County, Mississippi
roots.note: The supplied audit traces the tester to James J, not to a proved father for James. Its Wilson exclusion and proposed Robert-2769 attachment remain source-reported conclusions, not new findings of this revision.

roots.name: Alexander Glasgow
roots.route: County Antrim / Killoquin–Lisnagaver → Scotland; spouse reported as Mary McCaughen
roots.note: The Killoquin/Lisnagaver reference line. A second documented son-line could separate variants inherited by Alexander from mutations in later generations. Birth, route and spouse details are retained as reported.

roots.name: Robert Glasgow
roots.route: Glasgow-12 descendant lines → Pennsylvania, Ohio and Nebraska
roots.note: Four Big Y and two marker tests are grouped under the reported Robert-1749 family. The source calls 959947 documented, 200475 probable, and the two FTE32242 tests separate son-lines of James M.

kits.name: Alexander Churnside
kits.label: Churnside · Jamaica
kits.pedigree: Tester-reported Churnside line: Jamaica in the match screen; Berwickshire ancestry and profile mapping supplied by the project timeline. Collateral R-FTA30932 branch below R-FT4811.

kits.name: Dixon Brown
kits.label: Dixon Brown · Virginia → Kentucky
kits.pedigree: Reported Virginia → Kentucky pedigree. R-FTA30932 is collateral to the Glasgow/Duffield path below R-FT4811; a Berwickshire origin for Brown is not established by the supplied root.

matches.name: James J Glasgow-2738 line
matches.description: Documented tester line; James's father unproved
matches.label: Big Y · R-FT20271
matches.interpretation: Nearest supplied Y-111 match to B580327 (GD 3). DYS714=27 supports a pairing hypothesis; no shared named child SNP is exposed.

matches.name: Wm Farrier and Susanna Abell line
matches.description: Philadelphia marriage reported in 1796 · match A
matches.label: Y-111 · R-M269
matches.interpretation: Useful cross-surname lead. A broad R-M269 label does not establish FT20271 membership.

matches.name: Wm Farrier and Susanna Abell line
matches.description: Philadelphia marriage reported in 1796 · match B
matches.label: Y-111 · R-M269
matches.interpretation: Second test with the same reported Farrier–Abell root; do not count it as an independent old lineage without a pedigree audit.

matches.name: Reported William c.1655 line
matches.description: Scotland · historical root not independently proved
matches.label: Big Y · R-FT20271
matches.interpretation: GD 5 on Y-111; lowest reported extended-STR mismatch count, 3/650. These are different measurements.

matches.name: Henry Ferrier, born c.1758
matches.label: Y-111 · R-M269
matches.interpretation: Another close Farrier/Ferrier lead; terminal SNP placement is unknown.

matches.name: Glasgow line
matches.label: Y-111 · R-M269
matches.interpretation: An STR match with no named historical anchor in the supplied screen.

matches.name: James M. Glasgow, 1799–1875
matches.description: through son Glasgow-2182 · confirmed FTE32242 test A
matches.label: Big Y · R-FTE32242
matches.interpretation: FTE32242-assigned descendant through William Allen. Its Y-111 state is identical to basal kit 200475.

matches.name: Robert Glasgow, 1749–1839
matches.label: Big Y · R-FT20271
matches.interpretation: FT20271-assigned John M. line. The supplied audit labels the final private continuation probable.

matches.name: Robert Glasgow, 1749–1839
matches.label: Y-111 · R-Z18
matches.interpretation: Reported Glasgow-12 pedigree. R-Z18 does not resolve membership in a recent child branch.

matches.name: James M. Glasgow, 1799–1875
matches.description: through son Glasgow-192 · confirmed FTE32242 test B
matches.label: Big Y · R-FTE32242
matches.interpretation: FTE32242-assigned descendant through Samuel Lyle; a second reported son-line of James M.

matches.name: Documented William Glasgow branch
matches.description: Robert Glasgow-12 descendant · final link verified in the 1950 census
matches.label: Big Y · R-FT20271
matches.interpretation: William son-line described as documented in the supplied audit. FT6135 is displayed derived; other son-lines need direct calls.

matches.name: Alexander Churnside, 1838–1873
matches.label: Big Y · R-FTA30932
matches.interpretation: Collateral paternal kin through R-FT4811: FTA30932 is the Churnside/Brown sister branch to the FT32941 → Glasgow path. The timeline’s Berwickshire lead adds medieval geographic context; Jamaica is the match-screen root location.

matches.name: Henry Glasgo, 1774–1849
matches.label: Big Y · R-FT25406
matches.interpretation: Unnumbered Big Y assigned to FT25406. Do not transfer this assignment to kit 325862.

matches.name: Henry Glasgo, 1774–1849
matches.label: Y-111 · R-M269
matches.interpretation: A separate Henry-root Y-111 kit; terminal SNP status remains unresolved.

matches.name: Phillips line
matches.label: Y-111 · R-M269
matches.interpretation: Unplaced cross-surname STR match without an earliest ancestor in this screen.

matches.name: Dixon Brown, 1758–1828
matches.label: Big Y · R-FTA30932
matches.interpretation: Shares R-FTA30932 with the Churnside line and joins the Glasgow/Duffield path at R-FT4811. Useful evidence for the wider medieval family, not a branch inside FT20271 or proof that Brown came from Berwickshire.

matches.name: Robert Glasgow, c.1710–after 1772
matches.label: Y-111 · R-M269
matches.interpretation: High-value East Antrim testing candidate, but historical root mapping and terminal SNP placement remain distinct questions.

markers.name: DYS714
markers.note: Shared by Alexander and James J in this seven-kit set. This is the marker used by SAPP Node 17.

markers.name: DYS576
markers.note: Observed endpoints. Ancestral 16 and the two separate changes are SAPP assumptions, not observed history.

markers.name: DYS561
markers.note: A reported James J-line departure within this set.

markers.name: DYS19
markers.note: Part of the three-state Glasgow-12 motif.

markers.name: DYS456
markers.note: Part of the three-state Glasgow-12 motif.

markers.name: DYS712
markers.note: Part of the three-state Glasgow-12 motif; still an STR state, not a named SNP.

markers.name: DYS389II
markers.note: Reported composite DYS389II values. DYS389I must be accounted for before recomputing general distances.

markers.name: DYS650
markers.note: The page explicitly compares the Glasgow-12 family here; unrelated values have not been filled in.

markers.name: CDY
markers.note: A terminal difference inside the FTE32242 family. Other lines are not filled from assumption.

sources.title: Azimi et al. · The maximum four point condition matrix of a tree
sources.detail: The two largest quartet sums must agree for distances to be additive on a tree. This is applied to the supplied matrix, not to DNA reads.
sources.date: 2023 paper; checked 6 Sep 2026

sources.title: Seven-kit matrix audit
sources.detail: All 21 distances retained; symmetry and triangle inequalities checked. Eight minimum spanning trees of weight 15; four of 35 quartet tests fail exact additivity. The matrix is not a direct mutation-history tree.
sources.date: Calculated 6 Sep 2026

sources.title: Glasgow project · supplied Y-DNA Timeline
sources.detail: Pasted text(20260906-210826).txt. Supplies S14827 → FTC49014 → FT4811 context, the FT4811 collateral branches, reported age estimates and the North Sea / Norman / Scottish / Ulster narrative. Source sections: S14827 (lines 1450–1546), FT4811 (1549–1653), FTC49014 (1655–1693), FT32941 (1694–1797), FT25406 (1799–1888), FT20271 (1891–2015). Project-specific genetic ages and medieval-person claims were not independently re-verified. An unchanged copy is retained in the source archive.
sources.date: Supplied 6 Sep 2026

sources.title: FamilyTreeDNA · Understanding the Discover Time Tree
sources.detail: Time Tree ages concern common ancestors and branching. Country labels are self-reported paternal origins of testers; they are not direct medieval geolocation. The specific live FT4811, FTA30932 and FT32941 pages could not be retrieved in this revision, so their project-supplied values remain a snapshot.
sources.date: Reference retained from earlier 6 Sep 2026 build

sources.title: Derbyshire Historic Environment Record · Duffield Castle (MDR4704)
sources.detail: The official monument record summarises excavation evidence for a de Ferrers earth-and-timber castle around 1080, followed by the later stone keep. This independently anchors the proposed medieval setting, not the genotype, ancestry or occupation of any Glasgow/Duffield man.
sources.date: Reference retained from earlier 6 Sep 2026 build

sources.title: City of Edinburgh Council · early royal burghs
sources.detail: The council describes David I’s twelfth-century burgh programme, including Berwick and Stirling, and cites a 1127 charter reference to Edinburgh. Useful context for movement into Scottish administrative and trading centres; not proof of the project’s Huntingdon or Glasgow pedigree.
sources.date: Reference retained from earlier 6 Sep 2026 build

sources.title: Narrative edition · explanatory reconstruction
sources.detail: Reorganises the supplied evidence into five connected story chapters. Adds branch explanations, three-level family inheritance highlights and qualitative route comparisons. Source measurements, SNP calls, missing states and reported age ranges are retained. The c.1066–1150 arrival model is the project timeline’s historical scenario, not a newly calculated probability or date interval.

sources.title: Yorkshire Pipe Roll · Roger de Duffeld, Michaelmas 1194
sources.detail: The Great Roll of the Pipe for Richard I's sixth regnal year, Yorkshire, p. 150: Rogerus de Duffeld owed half a mark because he did not produce the person for whom he had acted as pledge. This is a fiscal/surety entry, not a 1190 poll tax, land grant, castle office or Scottish record.
sources.date: 1194 record; documentary audit refreshed 7 Sep 2026

sources.title: Registrum Episcopatus Glasguensis · Bishop Jocelin's charter no. 41
sources.detail: The act names Master John of Huntingdon in Bishop Jocelin's household and Roger de Glasgu among the witnesses to a grant involving a Glasgow burgh toft and Clyde fishing right. Their joint occurrence proves association in one episcopal-property network, not kinship or a change of surname.
sources.date: c.1175–1199 act; printed 1843; audit refreshed 7 Sep 2026

sources.title: Glasgow University Archives BL/204 · John de Glasgow alias Smith
sources.detail: Catalogue description of the 28 April 1506 instrument: Agnes, daughter and heir of Robert Watson, disposed a four-shilling High Street annual rent to Sir Allan Smith and John de Glasgow alias Smith. The complete instrument remains unread; no occupation or relationship between Allan and John is stated.
sources.date: 1506 instrument; catalogue audit refreshed 7 Sep 2026

sources.title: Liber Collegii Nostre Domine · Glasgow Saltmarket title trail
sources.detail: The printed register identifies a four-shilling annual on John Glasgow's Saltmarket tenement in 1527 and places William Glasgow in the same title position by 1528/29. Later boundaries and rentals preserve the parcel. The succession is strong property evidence but contains no father-son formula and has not been linked to the separate 1506 alias-Smith rent.
sources.date: 1527–1548 records; audit refreshed 7 Sep 2026

sources.type: Published charter text and digital index
sources.title: Paisley register · the two Alexander sons of Richard, 1283
sources.detail: DEEDS 06190338 and 06190340 distinguish Alexander, son of the late Richard the messenger of Glasgow, from Alexander, son of Richard the former constable of Glasgow. The occupational/location phrases describe the fathers and do not by themselves establish an inherited Glasgow surname.
sources.date: 1283 acts; audit integrated 7 Sep 2026

sources.title: Bain, Calendar of Documents Relating to Scotland II, no. 409
sources.detail: Calendars the mutilated 7 March 1289/90 receipt involving Alexander, escheator south of the Forth, with old locator Chapter House (Scots Documents), Box 94, no. 5. The original and current TNA reference remain unchecked.
sources.date: 1289/90 record; audit integrated 7 Sep 2026

stages.title: The older family belongs to the North Sea world.
stages.summary: The deep Z17–S20045 ancestry provides the long background. The more focused clue is S14827’s northern sister lines, which keep the Glasgow story connected to a wider Scandinavian and North Sea family.
stages.genetic: The source path runs Z17 → S20045 → BY139800 → S14827. Its long, sparsely branching stretch is the starting point for the timeline’s survival-and-expansion narrative.
stages.geography: The later BY61198 and BY136156 sister lines include Swedish, Danish and Norwegian paternal roots. These give the project specific cousin branches to compare with the path towards Britain.
stages.reading: Picture several related paternal lines developing within a sea-connected northern world. Some later family histories remain Scandinavian; another part of the tree eventually supplies the British-linked branches. That contrast matters more to the route question than any single broad haplogroup label.
stages.next: Earlier sourced paternal places and new, well-resolved basal cousins can refine where the branches were rooted.

stages.title: The connecting branch is where the journey belongs.
stages.summary: S14827 and the timeline’s FTC49014 node connect the older northern family to FT4811. This is the genetic stretch across which the project explores direct North Sea movement and a longer route through Normandy.
stages.genetic: S14827 is estimated around 379 CE, with a reported range of 72 BCE–741 CE. FTC49014 is labelled around 500 CE. The tree gives these generations a place even when the family records have not survived.
stages.geography: A direct early British crossing, Norse-era movement and continental settlement before a Norman-era arrival all start within the broader northern geography described by the timeline.
stages.reading: A family split and a migration can be separated by many generations. The useful task is to reconstruct the geographic history of the descendant branch: which cousins stayed nearby, which developed elsewhere, and where later families first enter the record.
stages.next: Compare the earliest places associated with lines close to FTC49014 and FT4811, including continental as well as British roots.

stages.title: The medieval fork produces several later surnames.
stages.summary: FT4811 brings together the tested ancestors of Churnside/Brown, Glasgow and the Wright line. A separate project page reports a Duffield line on FT32941, but its kit identity, placement evidence and pedigree are not present in this dataset.
stages.genetic: FT4811 is estimated around 1044 CE, with the source’s 95% range of 697–1313. FTA30932 and FT32941 are different child branches; Glasgow continues on the FT32941 side.
stages.geography: Duffield Castle supplies a genuine de Ferrers setting in Derbyshire, but Roger de Duffeld’s inspected record is a 1194 Yorkshire Pipe Roll entry and his locative could derive from North or South Duffield. Churnside’s Berwickshire lead, Brown’s American root and Wright’s later London anchor remain separate paper trails.
stages.reading: The genetic fork reconnects modern paternal lines; it does not identify their medieval surnames or households. The Norman/Ferrers route remains one mechanism to test alongside earlier British and Norse alternatives. The modern Farrier/Ferrier STR matches are a separate question from the medieval de Ferrers family.
stages.next: Verify the reported Duffield FT32941 result and pedigree, inspect collateral roots, and use a Big Y upgrade to place one of the three Farrier/Ferrier Y-111 matches.

stages.title: The paternal path narrows into the Scottish surname.
stages.summary: FT32941 is ancestral to FT25406, which gathers the tested Glasgow/Glasgo lines. The documentary audit asks whether English-associated church or burgh networks can explain the Scottish surname without treating the reported Duffield placement as already verified.
stages.genetic: FT25406 has an estimated common ancestor around 1431, with a reported range of 1199–1608. It gives the wider Glasgow family an older shared node above the FT20271 lines.
stages.geography: Master John of Huntingdon served in Bishop Jocelin’s Glasgow household, where Roger de Glasgu already used the locative in the same charter. Later records place separate Glasgow bearers in church, royal, burgh and property settings from 1259 to 1506.
stages.reading: John of Huntingdon demonstrates a real English-associated clerical route into Glasgow, but his contemporary Roger de Glasgu prevents a simple ‘John changed his name’ story. At the later end, the Glasgow burgess of 1447–1455, the Stirling witness of 1475–1479/80, John alias Smith in 1506 and the Saltmarket holder from 1527 remain separate identities until property or kinship connects them.
stages.next: Seek explicit kinship or title succession. Obtain BL/204 in full, keep the 1506 alias rent separate from the 1527 Saltmarket parcel, and test the reported Duffield DNA placement independently.

stages.title: The younger family connects Scotland and Ulster.
stages.summary: FT20271 gathers the tested lines behind several Scottish, Ulster and American family histories. Its early-modern age gives those later movements a common paternal context.
stages.genetic: FT20271, FGC5690 and FT16542 form the supplied block. The common-ancestor estimate is 1583, with a reported range of 1387–1728. Five tests remain at this level and two share the younger FTE32242 branch.
stages.geography: The reported roots include County Antrim, Derry and Scotland. Different families can remain, move between Scotland and Ulster, or cross the Atlantic in later generations.
stages.reading: Think of a family expanding through several households rather than one traveller following every later route. The genetic node brings their histories into the same frame; individual papers can explain how religion, land, work and relatives shaped each movement.
stages.next: Place the older Kilwaughter lines with SNP tests and compare them with the known Antrim and Derry branches.

stages.title: The large historical picture becomes a set of named family questions.
stages.summary: The American and Ulster descendants now give the project actual family structures to compare: the Alexander–James J pairing, the Robert-1749 family and the older Henry Glasgo split.
stages.genetic: Alexander and James J share the DYS714=27 pattern. Robert’s four tests share a three-marker signature, and FTE32242 resolves the James M. branch within his reported pedigree.
stages.geography: The source follows separate American roots through South Carolina, Pennsylvania, Ohio and other destinations, alongside the Antrim-to-Scotland reference line. Each location opens a different set of family records.
stages.reading: The Atlantic dispersal separates relatives geographically but gives the research more descendant branches to test. A shared variant recovered through two well-traced lines can bring a missing ancestor’s part of the family into focus.
stages.next: Compare the existing close-match bundles and recruit descendants who branch at useful earlier generations.
